objection: Could the Bible have been changed to make Jesus divine?
answer:
I appreciate you separating two genuinely different questions — textual variants and theological development — because they need different answers.

On the variants: yes, the Comma Johanneum and the Markan long ending are late, and responsible scholarship (and the material I'm working from) doesn't lean on them. But notice the load-bearing texts for Christ's deity are not among the disputed readings. John 1:1, John 1:18, and John 20:28 are secured by P52 (c. AD 125), and P66/P75 (c. 200) — manuscripts older than any council, older than most of the "corruption" theory's imagined editorial window. If scribes were inserting deity into the text over time, we'd expect the earliest fragments to show a lower Christology than the later ones. Instead P52 and P75 already carry the highest material. That's the opposite of what a gradual-corruption theory predicts.

On development: here the passages push back harder than you'd expect. The "developmental line" you're describing — exaltation, then pre-existence, then full deity — was the old scholarly consensus, but it's been substantially abandoned, not because of apologetic pressure but because the earliest datable Christian material (creedal fragments, hymns, devotional practice) already shows the high end. Larry Hurtado's work on binitarian worship — prayer to Jesus, hymns to Jesus, baptism into his name — traces this to within the first years of the movement, among Jewish monotheists, which is the least likely soil for casual deification. Richard Bauckham's point sharpens this: the categories used (Creator, bearer of the Name, recipient of worship) are precisely the ones Judaism used to fence off God from every creature, and the NT writers include Jesus inside that fence from the start, not at the end of a trajectory.

As for the Paul/Mark/John contrast: it's true the Synoptics and John emphasize different things, and I won't pretend they read identically — that's a fair observation about genre and emphasis, not proof of absent belief. But Paul's letters predate the Gospels, and the material here notes that confession of Jesus as Lord and God is embedded in pre-Pauline tradition itself — meaning the "earliest layer" isn't Mark's low Christology gradually escalating to John's high one, but a high confession already presupposed before Paul writes anything. Where I'll concede a real gap: this material doesn't walk through a verse-by-verse comparison of Mark's implicit Christology against John's explicit "I am" sayings, so I won't manufacture an argument that isn't here. What it does support is that the trajectory you're proposing — low to high across time — doesn't match when the highest claims are actually first attested, in text or in worship.

transcript.content: Look, you've got a manuscript tradition stretching back to the second century—we have fragments from P52, P66, P75—and yet we also have *thousands* of variants, some of them touching exactly the Christological claims you're relying on. The longer ending of Mark, the Comma Johanneum, the "God" in 1 Timothy 3:16—these are all disputed or late additions. More fundamentally, though: if early Christians were actively *editing* the text to make Jesus divine, why do the *earliest* sources show the least explicit claims? Paul doesn't say Jesus claimed to be God; Mark doesn't have the "I am" sayings; only John does. Shouldn't it work the other way around—shouldn't the *oldest* copies be the most Christianized, not the newest? Instead we see a clean developmental line: exaltation, then pre-existence, then full deity. That's not textual corruption; that's theological evolution, captured in real time across our manuscripts.
